specAnchors.text: understand how the results of experiments involving the dilution of coloured solutions and diffusion of gases can be explained

primer.text: You already know from States of Matter that everything is made of particles, moving differently in solids, liquids and gases. This note turns that model into evidence: two classic experiments, the spread of bromine gas and the fading of a purple solution, only make sense if tiny moving particles really exist. Diffusion and dilution are the particle theory made visible.

modules.title: Diffusion
modules.opening: Release bromine gas at the bottom of a jar and, within minutes, the red-brown colour has climbed into a second jar above it. Nothing stirred the gas, yet its particles travelled on their own. That self-driven spreading is called diffusion, and it happens in liquids as well as gases.
keyPoints: Diffusion happens in gases and liquids because their particles are in random motion.
Particles travel from regions of high concentration towards regions where it is low.
Given time, the particles end up evenly spread throughout the available space.
Diffusion needs no energy input, but it speeds up at higher temperatures.
It is slower in liquids than in gases because liquid particles are closely packed and move slowly.

low.restatement: Gas and liquid particles wander randomly, so they drift away from crowded regions into emptier ones until they are spread out evenly.
low.analogy: It is like perfume crossing a quiet room, or a drop of food colouring creeping through still water, with nobody stirring anything.
low.examPointer: Learn the direction of spread, high concentration to low, and that diffusion happens on its own with no energy input.

medium.restatement: Random particle motion carries particles from where they are crowded to where they are scarce, and the spread continues until the concentration is even; heat speeds it up because hotter particles carry more kinetic energy.
medium.analogy: Picture commuters spilling from a packed platform into an empty concourse until everyone stands evenly spaced, and moving faster still when they hurry.
medium.examPointer: The bromine jar experiment is the classic evidence that all matter is made of tiny moving particles, which is what the spec asks you to explain.

modules.title: Dilution
modules.opening: Add water to a purple solution and the colour fades step by step, yet it survives many dilutions before it finally disappears. Dilution does not destroy or remove anything: it spreads the same solute particles further apart. How long that faint colour lasts is itself evidence that enormous numbers of very small particles make up even one crystal.
keyPoints: Dilution means adding more solvent, typically water, to an existing solution.
Adding solvent lowers the concentration of the solute particles in the solution.
The solute particles end up more widely separated yet remain in the solution.
The colour grows fainter with each dilution but does not disappear immediately.
The lasting faint colour shows a small crystal must contain a huge number of tiny particles.

low.restatement: Pour in more water and the same coloured particles spread through a bigger volume, so the colour looks fainter with every dilution.
low.analogy: It is like stirring a spoonful of squash into a whole bathtub: the colour is still there, just spread thin through the whole tub.
low.examPointer: Say that dilution spreads particles rather than removing them; the surviving tint is the evidence.

medium.restatement: Each addition of solvent lowers the concentration because the solute particles occupy a larger volume, and the tint survives many dilutions, showing how numerous and small the particles must be.
medium.analogy: Think of the squash again: a whole bathtub still shows a faint tint, so a single spoonful must hold an enormous number of tiny particles.
medium.examPointer: Dilution experiments on coloured solutions, like diffusion experiments on gases, support the kinetic theory of matter.

glossary.definition: The spreading of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
How crowded particles are within a given volume of gas or liquid.
The energy of motion; hotter particles carry more of it, so diffusion speeds up.
The process of adding more solvent to a solution, which lowers the concentration.
The liquid, usually water, that is added to dilute a solution.
The dissolved substance whose particles are spread further apart during dilution.
The mixture formed when a solute is dissolved in a solvent.

workedExample.prompt: Bromine vapour is released at the bottom of a sealed jar of air. In a second experiment, purple potassium manganate(VII) solution is diluted with more water. a) Name the process that spreads the bromine and state the direction the particles move. b) Explain why the bromine spreads through the whole jar with no stirring. c) State what happens to the colour as water is added, and what this kind of experiment is evidence for.
steps: a) The bromine spreads by diffusion: its particles move from the region of high concentration at the bottom towards the low-concentration region above.
b) Gas particles are in continuous random motion, so bromine and air particles mix on their own until the bromine is evenly spread through the available space; no energy input is required.
c) Adding water lowers the concentration of the purple particles, so the colour grows fainter with each dilution but does not vanish at once.
Diffusion and dilution experiments like these are evidence for the kinetic theory of matter — enormous numbers of very tiny, constantly moving particles.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Diffusion, from high to low concentration. b) Random particle motion spreads the gas evenly with no energy input. c) The colour fades gradually over repeated dilutions; such experiments evidence the kinetic theory of matter.
